newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rates inch higher, but analysts positive.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rates inch higher, but analysts positive.

text.p: Mexico's interest rates rose slightly during the weekly Cetes auction on Tuesday after weeks of big declines on foreign investor cheer about Mexico's improving economy.
Analysts said the small rise in rates was expected, particularly after a recent rally in U.S. Treasuries lost steam this week and started to pressure the Mexican peso.
Some investors also may be keeping to the sidelines before Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo's annual Informe, or State of the Nation address, on Sunday.
Despite the rise, analysts were positive about Mexican markets and said rates were as steady as anyone dared hope for right now.
"It was a good auction. Demand is healthy and rates are very steady," said Hector Chavez, director of analysis at Santander Investments in Mexico City.
Foreign investor appetite for Mexican paper continued due to expectations that inflation would keep falling even as the economy began to recover from a two-year recession, analysts said.
Despite rising long-term U.S. interest rates, rates on Mexico's bellwether 28-day Cetes rose just five basis points to 24.38 percent.
Medium-term rates rose more because of traditional jitters ahead of early November, when the government outlines its economic program for the following year.
Demand was a healthy 11.70 billion pesos at the auction.
The only potentially dark cloud on an otherwise clear horizon for Mexican paper are U.S. markets, analysts said.
U.S. economic data due out shortly could confirm fears the U.S. economy is growing too quickly and fanning inflation, analysts said.
"There is reason to be optimistic on the domestic front in Mexico. On the international front, there are risks," said Denis Parisien, an analyst at consultancy I.D.E.A. in New York.
Even if U.S. data was negative, Mexico might have enough going for it to escape the fallout that normally hits Latin American markets when U.S. rates begin to climb, analysts said.
"Mexico has become the regional favourite right now ... inflation should remain subdued ... and macroeconomic figures should be supportive," Parisien said.
Short-term rates in Mexico have probably hit a floor while longer rates still offer real returns, analysts said.
"I don't see short-term rates moving much in the next few weeks," said Chavez.

Zedillo's Informe should produce few surprises, analysts said. The president would likely hail the beginning of an economic recovery, pledge to continue monetary and fiscal prudence and promise to spend the government's fiscal surplus during the year's second half, analysts said.
Mexican stocks raced ahead on Tuesday in part because of expectations ahead of the Informe. Next week, stocks and paper could be set for some light profit-taking, analysts said.
